div.head: WHETHER THE AFFECTIONS OF THE SOUL ARE WORSE THAN THOSE OF THE BODY (ANIMINE AN CORPORIS AFFECTIONES SINT PEIORES)
INTRODUCTION
div.p: This popular oration, or diatribe, So Pohlenz, as I think, correctly: I therefore do not accept Wilamowitz’s combination of this and the preceding work as fragments of the same dialogue. was read by PlutarchXylander, practically alone, denies the genuineness - on what ground he does not say. in some city of Asia Minor: Volkmann Plutarch, vol. i. 62 f. thought Sardis, the capital of the province; Haupt Opuscula, iii. 554 (Hermes, vi. 258). thought Halicarnassus; Wilamowitz Hermes, xl. 161 ff. Ephesus. The occasion is clearly the consul’s yearly hearing of lawsuits from the whole province.
The proof that afflictions of the soul are worse than diseases of the body is treated in a popular and, in chapter 4, dramatic manner. The conclusion is lost.

The same subject was treated in his commonplace fashion by Maximus Tyrius, Orat. 7 ed. Hobein, 13 ed. Dübner. who shows no knowledge of Plutarch’s oration, nor any relation to his sources; Cicero, however, at the beginning of the third book of the Tusculan Disputations, exhibits some kinship with Plutarch’s argument. Siefert Comm. Ienenses, 1896, pp. 106-110; Plutarchs Schrift Περὶ εὐθυμίας, pp. 26-28. has twice elaborated his opinion that some of this work of
Plutarch’s was drawn from the ὑπόμνημα (I should prefer to say ὑπομνήματα See the introduction to the De Tranquillitate.) which Plutarch used in writing De Tranquillitate.
The text is not good. The work is listed as No. 208 in the Lamprias catalogue.

Homer, Il., xvii. 446-447; cf. 496 b, supra. having contemplated the mortal varieties of animals and having compared them with each other in respect to their lives and habits, cried out that nothing is
More wretched than man,
Of all that breathes and creeps upon the earth, awarding to man an unfortunate primacy in excess of evils. But as for us, as though acknowledging that man has won the victory in wretchedness and has been proclaimed the most miserable of animals, let us compare him with himself, dividing body and soul for competition of their individual miseries, a task not unprofitable but even quite necessary, to the end that we may learn whether it is through
